claim_notes.A: Key shape confirmed exactly: `${retained.streamEpoch}:${retained.sourceSeq}:${ordinal}` at SessionManager.ts:8534 (has() at 8537, add() at 8541), stored as `committedFactKeys: Set<string>` on RetainedTerminalSessionState (type decl ~635, isolation-snapshot type decl ~484). ADD: line 8541 (detectAndAppendRetainedTerminalFacts). DELETE: line 8255 inside removeRetainedTerminalFacts (per-key delete on ledger eviction, keyed the same way from evicted fact records). CLEAR: three call sites — line 3215 (ordinal-rollover branch that also bumps streamEpoch), line 8184 (disable-all-retained-tracking sweep over every session). Additionally there are two whole-set copy sites that are NOT plain add/delete/clear: line 5534 clones the set into a debug-isolation snapshot (`new Set(retained.committedFactKeys)`), and line 5964 restores the whole set wholesale from that snapshot (`retained.committedFactKeys = new Set(original.committedFactKeys)`) as part of TerminalAuthorityDebugIsolationState cleanup — this is a test/debug harness path, not organic runtime traffic. Everything checks out as claimed.
claim_notes.B: Confirmed on both parts. (1) Epoch direction: rollbackSession (TerminalAuthorityProductionAdapter.ts:4382) computes `nextStreamEpoch = nextOrdinal(state.streamEpoch)` (nextOrdinal is a strict BigInt+1, TerminalAuthorityProductionAdapter.ts:923) and TerminalAuthorityController.beginRollback (TerminalAuthorityController.ts:1451) additionally hard-rejects with `rollback-identity-invalid` unless `ordinalGreaterThan(request.nextStreamEpoch, state.streamEpoch)` holds — so the shipping path cannot roll back to an equal or lower epoch; it is enforced twice, not just asserted by convention. (2) committedFactKeys contact: neither rollbackSession nor beginRollback nor SessionManager.beginTerminalAuthorityRollback (SessionManager.ts:5371, a pure delegation to controller.beginRollback) references committedFactKeys anywhere — grep across TerminalAuthorityProductionAdapter.ts and TerminalAuthorityController.ts returns zero hits for that identifier. The set is untouched by the shipping rollback path itself; it only gets cleared later, indirectly, when the post-rollback stream advance eventually crosses an ordinal-rollover boundary (SessionManager.ts:3215) — a separate mechanism, not something rollback triggers directly.
claim_notes.C: Refuted as an exclusive claim, though the core assertion about `responder.active` being the primary single-valued arbiter for the *hazard* property is correct. The two query-reply guards do NOT check `responder.active` alone: writeTerminalAuthorityServerQueryReply (SessionManager.ts:5391) requires `runtime.admission.mode === 'server' && runtime.responder.active === 'server-headless' && runtime.responder.activeLeaseId === input.responderLeaseId && runtime.responder.serverEnabled && !revokedLeaseIds.has(...)` — five conjuncts including the boolean `serverEnabled`. writeTerminalAuthorityCompatibilityQueryReply (SessionManager.ts:5408) checks eight conjuncts including `responder.legacyEnabled` plus driver-lease/view-generation state. So arbitration is by a compound guard, not a single field; `serverEnabled`/`legacyEnabled` are load-bearing conditions in the guards themselves, not vestigial. What IS true and matches the claim's spirit: at all twelve sites in SessionManager.ts that assign these two booleons, `responder.active` is assigned first in the same block, so the *simultaneous-both-true* hazard the exclusivity test cares about is structurally excluded by the active-field convention even if one of the two booleans were (hypothetically) left stale — but the query-reply guards as written still read the booleans, so a bug that flips only one boolean while leaving `active` correct WOULD currently be caught by these two functions returning false, contradicting the premise that the booleans are non-arbitrating vestiges.
